taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes no subspecies are recognized.
fieldMarks: Long striped garter snake, usually 40-70 cm (occasionally to 109 cm), dark brown to dark greenish with a dorsal and two lateral yellow or orange stripes.
Lateral stripes lie on scale rows 3 and 4; some red pigment may show on the sides.
A row of black spots runs between each lateral stripe and the belly scales.
Keeled scales in 19-21 rows and an undivided anal plate; males have tubercles on the chin shields and slightly longer tails.
behavior: Active March-November depending on region; hibernates in rodent or ant burrows, rock crevices and human-made crevices and may emerge on warm winter days.
Diurnal at 21-29 C, switching to night activity above 31 C and becoming inactive in much colder weather.
Follows odour trails to prey, mates and hibernacula; eats frogs, toads, salamanders, fish, earthworms, small rodents and birds.
habitat: Meadows, prairies and other grasslands near ponds, streams, marshes and sloughs, also swampy areas, rivers and suburban vacant lots; where it overlaps the common gartersnake it uses drier habitat.
range: Great Plains from the Oklahoma panhandle, northern Texas and northeastern New Mexico north to southern Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and east through Minnesota, Wisconsin and Indiana.

lookalikes.name: Common gartersnake (Thamnophis sirtalis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Plains gartersnake's lateral stripe sits on scale rows 3 and 4; the common gartersnake's is on rows 2 and 3.
